title: I Followed the Hardware Store Return Policy Into the Ground

parts.text: I rang up eighteen gallons of mistinted paint at 4:55 p.m. and Don wanted them free. He has thirty years in trades and thinks my family store still owes his uncle a favor. I am forty-four, owner, tired of favors. The bell over the door still sticks in humidity. "Contractor discount," Don said, sliding a stained receipt from 2019. I said, "That discount died with the old register." He laughed too loud for the aisle. "Your dad would have done it." My dad also wrote NO RETURNS AFTER TINT on a card that still hangs by the shakers. Don pointed at it. "Then untint it." I looked at the cans, all a pinkish beige called Oyster Whisper. "I can't untint." He leaned on the counter, leaving a thumbprint in the dust I had just wiped. "Then I'll take them on account." We don't do accounts. I said so. He raised his voice so Mrs. Pell in fasteners could hear. "You're going to lose every contractor in this town." I printed the return policy, the one he made me laminate last spring after he returned a used saw. "All sales of tinted product are final," I read. He snatched the paper. "Fine. I'll return the empty cans tomorrow and you will honor receipts." I said, "Empty cans aren't a receipt." He smiled. "Watch me." He left the eighteen gallons on my counter like a threat. "He wants the forklift key. He says it's store policy that contractors can load themselves.".
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Don is using the contractor-loading rule to get into the yard, and the town chat is already calling for a freeze.

social.video_title: He wanted eighteen mistints free — Part 1/2
social.description: A stuck doorbell, Oyster Whisper pink, and a 2019 receipt waved like a crown. The contractor chat lit up before he even hit the parking lot. Would you have laminated that policy?

parts.text: I did not give him the forklift key. I walked to the yard gate with the laminated card and my phone on speaker. "Policy says contractors may load purchases," I said. "You didn't purchase." Don was already on the forklift, which meant someone had left the key in the ignition like we always did at 4:55. "Get down," I said. He lifted a pallet of paid lumber that was not his, just to prove the machine worked. Mrs. Pell filmed from the parking lot. I called the non-emergency line because a forklift in the hands of a man having a tantrum is not a vibe, it's a report. An officer I grew up with arrived, looked at the mistints, and looked at Don. "You stealing lumber, Don?" Don dropped the forks too fast. A bag of Quikrete split. Dust went everywhere, that dry concrete smell that stays in your nose. He yelled, "She's killing local business!" I held up the contractor chat screenshot. The officer asked Don to leave. The next morning three contractors came in for the Oyster Whisper at half off, which I had posted on the door, not the chat. Don's apprentice quit and asked for a job stocking. I hired him. I changed the forklift policy to keys in the office only, which Don himself had demanded in 2019 after a near miss. Mrs. Pell buys her screws here and tells the version where I was fair. I can live on fair.

social.video_title: He took the forklift over free paint — Part 2/2
social.description: The yard gate, a split bag of Quikrete, and a policy he wrote himself in 2019. Half-off mistints sold to everyone except the man who wanted them free. Was the freeze real?
